title: He looked untouchable.
paragraphs: He looked untouchable.
That’s always how it starts.

The throne.
The applause.
The influence.
The confidence that slowly mutates into something darker.
And then… the shift happens.
Not all at once.
Quietly.
A man stops trembling before God.
That’s the pattern.

Not weakness.
Not failure.
Not imperfection.
Pride.

The chilling pattern behind every man God removed from power was never merely political collapse, military defeat, or public scandal. It was spiritual corrosion hidden beneath success. A slow internal rebellion that eventually became visible for everyone to see.
And most people never recognize it until judgment arrives.
But God saw it.
You knew.

The terrifying part is this:
many of these men once walked closely with God.

They were chosen.
Anointed.
Gifted.
Used mightily.
And still removed.
Because God is not impressed by titles, crowds, gifting, influence, or longevity.
He looks at the heart.

“God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”
— James 4:6
Read that again.
Opposes.

Not ignores.
Not warns repeatedly forever.
Opposes.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.
Saul is one of the clearest examples.
When Saul first appeared in Scripture, he looked humble. He even hid among the baggage when Samuel called him to be king.
But power revealed what was already growing inside him.

Insecurity became jealousy.
Jealousy became rage.
Rage became rebellion against God Himself.
At first, Saul disobeyed in what looked “small.”

A partial obedience here.
A rationalization there.
That’s how spiritual decay works.
It never announces itself dramatically in the beginning.
It whispers.

You deserve this.
You know better.
You can compromise just a little.
You can keep the appearance of obedience.
And Saul did exactly that.
God told him to completely destroy Amalek.
Saul kept what looked valuable.
Then he justified it spiritually.
That’s the dangerous stage.
When a man can sin while still sounding religious.
“But Samuel replied:

‘Does the Lord delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as much as in obeying the Lord? To obey is better than sacrifice… Because you have rejected the word of the Lord, He has rejected you as king.’
— 1 Samuel 15:22-23
The crown stayed on Saul’s head for a while after that.
But heaven had already removed him.
That should terrify every person pretending outward success means God’s approval.
Because sometimes judgment starts invisibly.
You can still have followers and already be abandoned spiritually.
You can still preach and already be empty.
You can still lead and already be rejected by God.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
The pattern repeats again and again through Scripture.
Nebuchadnezzar stood on his palace roof admiring Babylon and said:

“Is not this the great Babylon I have built… by my mighty power and for the glory of my majesty?”
— Daniel 4:30
The words were still in his mouth when judgment fell.
God reduced a king to madness.
Why?
Because pride always tries to steal glory that belongs to God alone.
And God will not share His glory with idols.
Not even when the idol is you.
Then came Herod.
The people shouted that his voice sounded like a god.
Instead of rejecting the worship, he absorbed it.

Loved it.
Fed on it.

“Immediately, because Herod did not give praise to God, an angel of the Lord struck him down.”
— Acts 12:23
Power intoxicates people who stop fearing God.
That’s the pattern.
Every man God removed from power reached the same spiritual condition:
they no longer saw themselves accurately.
Pride blinded them.
And pride is deadly because it convinces you that you are still right while you are drifting further into darkness.
Pharaoh hardened his heart repeatedly even after witnessing miracle after miracle.
Judas walked with Jesus Himself and still loved money more than truth.
King Uzziah started faithful, strong, and blessed.
But Scripture says:

“But after Uzziah became powerful, his pride led to his downfall.”
— 2 Chronicles 26:16
Read that again.
After he became powerful.
Success often reveals what suffering concealed.

Some people seek power believing it will complete them.
But power doesn’t create character.
It exposes it.
God saw it.
You knew.
And maybe this article stopped feeling like history halfway through.
Because the pattern isn’t only about kings.
It’s about us.
The terrifying truth is that every human heart naturally drifts toward self-glory apart from God.
That’s why pride is not merely a personality flaw.
It’s a sin problem.
A worship problem.
It’s humanity trying to replace God with self.
That’s been the rebellion since Eden.

“You will be like God.”
— Genesis 3:5
The same poison still runs through modern hearts.

You see it in the man who wants influence more than holiness.
The pastor who loves the platform more than prayer.
The husband who demands honor but refuses repentance.
The woman who wants blessing without surrender.
The believer who wants Jesus as Savior but not Lord.
And eventually the pattern leads somewhere.
Collapse.

Maybe public.
Maybe private.
Maybe eternal.
Because sin always promises elevation before destruction.

“Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall.”
— Proverbs 16:18
But this is where the Gospel changes everything.
Because Christianity is not a story about proud men climbing higher.
It is about a holy God humbling Himself to save rebels.
Jesus Christ had all authority, all glory, all power…
Yet He washed feet.
He served.
He surrendered Himself to the cross.
Philippians 2 says Christ “made Himself nothing” and became obedient unto death.
That’s the opposite pattern.
While proud men grasp for power, Jesus laid His down.
While sinful humanity exalts self, Christ humbled Himself.
And because of His sacrifice, even proud sinners can be forgiven.
That includes you.

No matter how far pride has corrupted your heart.
No matter how long you’ve performed religion while secretly resisting God.
No matter how many times you justified compromise.
Grace is still available.
But repentance is required.

Not image management.
Not public performance.
Not emotional words without surrender.
Real repentance.

The kind that says:
“God, I was wrong.”
“Break my pride.”
“Rule over my life.”
“Save me from myself.”
Because the same God who removed proud kings also gives mercy to the humble.
That’s the beauty of the Gospel.
Saul died clinging to his throne.
David fell horribly too—but David broke before God in repentance.
That’s the difference.
Not perfection.
Surrender.

One hardened.
One humbled himself.

One protected his image.
One cried, “Against You and You only have I sinned.”
And maybe that’s the crossroads in front of you now.
You can keep protecting pride until it destroys you.
Or you can bow before Christ while mercy is still being offered.
One path ends in collapse.
The other ends in redemption.
God saw it.
You knew.
